body_markdown:
Ferrari built just 10 NART Spiders, and only one of them went to movie star, car guy, and “King of Cool” Steve McQueen. That car just sold for[$18,925,000](https://www.goodingco.com/lot/1967-ferrari-275-gtb-4s-nart-spider?sortBy=ENDING_SOONEST&pageNumber=2) (including buyer’s premium) at an auction in New York City. Is that a lot of money? Of course. But, given the car that money bought and who the car’s first owner was, you could also answer that question, “Not really.”


Gooding Christie's


Ferrari started building its[275 GTB](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=ferrari+275+gtb) in 1964. Bodied by Scaglietti and powered by a 3.3-liter version of the Colombo V-12 engine mated to a five-speed transaxle, the model lasted until 1968. It was built in both short- and long-nose body styles, could be had with all-aluminum bodywork, and came with both two- and four-cam versions, but Ferrari made no plans to offer anything but a coupe. The mechanically similar drop-top[275 GTS](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/275_gts/1966/1966-ferrari-275_gts-base?id=aCn1I000000CwOySAK) had completely different, more conservative styling.


Enter Luigi Chinetti, the New York–based racer, owner of the North American Racing Team (NART), and Ferrari distributor. Knowing that his American customers enjoyed some sun on their faces and wind in their hair, he had helped convince Ferrari to build the California Spider on the 250 platform in the late ’50s, and he saw a similar opportunity with the 275 GTB, especially when the four-cam version debuted in late 1966. At Chinetti’s urging, a small batch of GTB/4s left Scaglietti sans roof. Chinetti sold them through his dealership, fitted with a not-so-subtle NART badge on the tail. “[NART Spider](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/275_gts!!4/1967/1967-ferrari-275_gts!!4-nart?id=aCn1I000000DUFZSA4) ” was never an official designation, but the name stuck.


Gooding Christie's


Gooding Christie's


While Chinetti thought he could sell 25 examples, only 10 were completed. The first chassis finished second in class at Sebring in 1967, got a repaint, and made the cover of *Road & Track* . The magazine called it “the most satisfying sports car in the world.” Another NART Spider appeared in the 1968 film *The Thomas Crown Affair* , starring Steve McQueen. The “red Italian thing” doesn’t get a ton of screen time, but it must have made an impression on the actor, because he went right out and bought this one—chassis 10453. The sixth NART Spider built, it crossed the Atlantic in the fall of ’67 finished in *Blu Sera* over black Connolly leather. McQueen, who personalized many of his cars to at least some degree, apparently didn’t like the color and had it repainted in a different shade of metallic blue. He also had the bumpers removed and an external quick-fill fuel cap installed, along with a smaller, rally-style mirror. The seats were also retrimmed with a different stitch pattern.


According to Gooding Christie’s, not long into McQueen’s ownership a truck hit the NART Spider from behind on the Pacific Coast Highway and pushed it into the car ahead, causing damage at both ends of that glorious Scaglietti shape. The car was soon repaired and repainted in the same metallic blue, modified with flared fenders and a flip-tail rear. Gooding also notes that the “surviving record does not establish how often McQueen drove his NART Spider or exactly when it left his possession, and no period photographs are known to show him with it.” McQueen didn’t keep it too long, as it was with another California owner by 1971. The current owner bought it from a Long Island Ferrari dealer in 1985, and it has remained in largely preserved condition ever since.


Gooding Christie's


This was the star car of Gooding Christie’s NYC auction this week, coinciding with the inaugural Retromobile New York, a classic car expo similar to the long-running Rétromobile Paris. Bidding opened at $10M and slowly worked its way to the $17.2M hammer price, which falls right within Gooding’s presale estimate range of $15M–$20M. The $18.9M final price makes it, by our count, the 31st most expensive car ever sold at auction.


A car as rare and sought after as the NART Spider tends to stay in long-term collector ownership, and public sales almost never happen. Another one did come to market in 2013, though, and it sold for the much higher sum of[$27,500,000](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo13/lots/r197-1967-ferrari-275-gtb4s-nart-spider-by-scaglietti/) . Unlike the blue car sold this week, it was a one-owner car with no accident history or modifications, and it boasted a full restoration.


It would have been reasonable to think that the blue car would’ve been able to make up for it with the Steve McQueen history. After all, multiple ex-McQueen cars and motorcycles have come to auction over the years, and they tend to bring a[big premium](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/the-hagerty-power-list-2022-movie-stars/) . One recent and fairly direct comparable is his 275 GTB coupe that sold in 2023 for[$5.4M](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mo23/lots/r0015-1967-ferrari-275-gtb4-by-scaglietti/) , nearly $2M more than the model’s condition #1 (concours) value in our price guide at the time. That said, the[market for vintage Ferraris](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-indexes-underscore-a-mixed-market/#h-ferrari-index) has been on the soft side this year, even as more modern Ferraris smash records and make headlines. It’s also possible that McQueen’s star is fading a bit. He died 46 years ago, and his biggest car film, *Le Mans* , came out 55 years ago.


But regardless of Enzo-era Ferrari pricing or whether someone can be the King of Cool forever, this is one of the most important and expensive cars sold anywhere this year.
